exams.title: Global Success 10 – Unit 1: Family Life – Test 1: Ngữ pháp & Từ vựng (15 câu)

qs.q:
UNIT 1: FAMILY LIFE — NGỮ PHÁP & TỪ VỰNG (ĐỀ 1): Mark the letter A, B, C, or D on your answer sheet to indicate the correct answer to each of the following questions.
In my family, my father usually ______ the heavy lifting, while my mother cooks dinner.
qs.ex: Thói quen ở hiện tại ('usually') dùng Hiện tại đơn; cụm cố định 'do the heavy lifting' (làm việc nặng).

qs.q: Listen! My sister ______ the piano in the living room while Mum is laying the table.
qs.ex: Dấu hiệu 'Listen!' ở đầu câu → Hiện tại tiếp diễn: is playing.

qs.q: Sharing household chores equally helps strengthen family ______ and teaches children responsibility.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 1: family bonds = sự gắn kết gia đình.

qs.q: As the primary ______ of the family, Mr Minh works hard to pay for his children’s school fees.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 1: breadwinner = người trụ cột đi làm kiếm tiền nuôi gia đình.

qs.q: My brother can’t answer the phone right now because he ______ out the rubbish.
qs.ex: Dấu hiệu 'right now' → Hiện tại tiếp diễn: is taking (take out the rubbish = đổ rác).

qs.q: Mrs Lan is a dedicated ______ who manages the home and raises three children.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 1: homemaker = người nội trợ chăm sóc gia đình.

qs.q: Every Sunday morning, my mother goes to the market to shop for ______.
qs.ex: Cụm từ Unit 1: shop for groceries = mua thực phẩm và đồ dùng thiết yếu.

qs.q: Parents ______ that children develop important life skills when they help with housework.
qs.ex: 'know' là động từ chỉ trạng thái nhận thức (stative verb), không chia ở thì tiếp diễn → dùng 'know'.

qs.q: After dinner, my younger brother clears the table and I ______ the washing-up.
qs.ex: Collocation Unit 1: do the washing-up = rửa bát đĩa.

qs.q: At the moment, our school Youth Union ______ a 'Share the Chores' campaign for all students.
qs.ex: Dấu hiệu 'At the moment' → Hiện tại tiếp diễn: is preparing.

qs.q: Children who share housework with their parents learn to show ______ to the people who care for them.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 1: show gratitude = thể hiện lòng biết ơn.

qs.q: My aunt ______ two loads of laundry every evening because she has three small children.
qs.ex: Dấu hiệu 'every evening' + cụm 'do the laundry' (giặt giũ) → does.

qs.q: Please be quiet! The baby ______ in the bedroom, and Mum is tidying the kitchen.
qs.ex: Dấu hiệu 'Please be quiet!' → hành động đang diễn ra: is sleeping.

qs.q: Doing housework together gives parents and children a chance to ______ and understand each other better.
qs.ex: Động từ Unit 1: bond = gắn kết tình cảm gia đình.

qs.q: Most teenagers in our class ______ helping their parents with the cooking at weekends.
qs.ex: 'like' là stative verb, đi với chủ ngữ số nhiều 'Most teenagers' → dùng 'like'.

qs.q:
Mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best arrangement of utterances or sentences to make a cohesive and coherent exchange or text in each of the following questions from 7 to 11.
**Dear Emma,**
a. On weekdays, my mother cooks dinner while my father cleans the kitchen, and I usually do the washing-up.
b. Thank you for your email; it was great to hear about your family.
c. At weekends, however, we do the housework together, and we always finish by having a family lunch.
d. I’m writing to tell you how we share the chores in my family.
e. Write back soon and tell me about the chores in your house!
**Best wishes,**
qs.ex: Trình tự bức thư chuẩn: Cảm ơn thư trước đó (b) → Nêu mục đích viết thư kể về việc chia sẻ việc nhà (d) → Kể việc nhà ngày thường (a) → Kể việc nhà cuối tuần (c) → Câu kết thư (e): b - d - a - c - e.

qs.q:
a. Mum: Yes, please. Could you take out the rubbish?
b. Mai: Mum, I’ve just finished the washing-up. Is there anything else I can do?
c. Mai: Sure. I’ll do it right now.
qs.ex: Trình tự hội thoại: Mai báo vừa rửa bát xong và hỏi mẹ còn việc gì cần giúp không (b) → Mẹ nhờ Mai đi đổ rác (a) → Mai đồng ý làm ngay (c): b - a - c.

qs.q:
a. In some households, family members now make a chart that shows everyone’s tasks for each week.
b. In many families, housework used to be seen as a woman’s job, while men were expected to earn the money.
c. Today, however, more women work full time, so families are rethinking who should do what at home.
d. As a result, the home becomes a place where all members feel valued and supported.
e. This simple system prevents arguments, because everybody knows exactly what they are responsible for.

**Read the passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 17 to 26.**

**WHO DOES THE CHORES? SHARING FAIRLY**
In most homes, chores are shared, but rarely equally. Statistics Canada reports that men now spend about 1.9 hours a day on housework, which is 24 minutes more than thirty years ago, yet women still spend about 2.8 hours, almost an hour more. In Britain, a study by University College London of around 8,500 couples found that only seven per cent <u>**divided**</u> the housework equally. Even when both partners have full-time jobs, women are far more likely to do many hours of household work each week.
The gap lies not only in the amount of work but also in its type. Statistics Canada notes that women tend to do routine and repetitive tasks such as cooking, cleaning, laundry and shopping, whereas men more often do occasional tasks such as taking out the rubbish, repairing the house and mowing the lawn. Routine tasks must be done every day, so they leave less free time. The London researchers add that many couples simply follow the patterns they saw in their parents’ homes, a habit that leaves women with a “second shift” when they come home from work.
Fortunately, attitudes are changing. **[I]** Most men in the London study agreed that housework should be shared, even though they did less than five hours a week themselves. **[II]** The gap was smallest in the few homes where the woman was the main breadwinner; there, men did as much as women. **[III]** Families can begin by talking openly about who does what and by giving every member, including children, a regular task. **[IV]** Small changes like these can turn chores from a source of argument into a habit of cooperation.
Sharing housework matters for more than fairness. Children who watch their parents divide chores fairly are likely to see this pattern as normal, and <u>**they**</u> may repeat it in their own homes one day. Chores also teach responsibility, cooperation and teamwork, so a home in which everyone contributes is not only cleaner but also happier.
(Adapted from HuffPost Canada – report on Statistics Canada’s “Women in Canada” data, and Earth.com – “Study shows that women are still doing most of the housework”)

**THE POWER OF SHARED FAMILY MEALS**
Sharing a meal seems too ordinary to deserve attention, yet a growing body of research suggests otherwise. According to The Family Dinner Project, studies link regular family dinners with healthier eating habits, higher self-esteem, stronger resilience and better grades. Conversation around the table even seems to build children’s vocabulary, and shared meals are also linked with improved mental health and stronger relationships. Put simply, the dinner table is where family members feed both their bodies and their relationships.
Despite these benefits, family meals are becoming less common. Civil Eats reports that <u>**they**</u> have declined by more than thirty per cent over the past three decades, and that only about a quarter of families with children eat together seven or more times a week. <u>**Busy schedules, long commutes and conflict inside the family can all prevent people from eating together.**</u> Even when people do sit at the same table, screens may replace conversation.
The good news is that a family dinner does not have to be perfect. The Family Dinner Project stresses that its goals are about real life, not perfection: <u>**regular**</u> dinners with food, fun and conversation about things that matter. Families can start by cooking together, playing simple games at the table and using conversation starters to get everyone talking. Free recipes, games and tools are available on the project’s website. One of its founders adds that children who know their family’s stories become more resilient and have higher self-esteem.
Of course, no single dinner will solve every family problem, and some families simply cannot eat together every night. That is not a reason to give up. Even one or two shared meals a week can create moments of connection, and the <u>**habit**</u> can grow slowly. What matters most is not the food on the plate but the attention people give one another while they eat.
(Adapted from The Family Dinner Project – thefamilydinnerproject.org, and Civil Eats – “The Family Dinner Project Wants to Help You Make Communal Meals Happen”)

**PARTNERSHIPS BETWEEN SCHOOLS AND FAMILIES IN UNIT 1: FAMILY LIFE**
Over the past two years, a research team from the National Institute of Education has tracked 1,500 high school students to evaluate how sharing household chores and strengthening family bonds affects teenager development. The study found that while nearly ninety per cent of family members valued household chores, only forty-two per cent <u>**sustained**</u> these routines throughout the entire school year. Students who tried to practise alone often gave up after a few weeks when exam pressure increased.
By contrast, learners whose families and teachers coordinated their guidance achieved far more durable results. In households where parents actively joined weekend activities to divide housework fairly at home, teenagers were twice as likely to teach children responsibility and teamwork. Researchers explained that shared routines reduce the feeling of isolation and turn abstract classroom advice into enjoyable daily habits. Moreover, consistent family involvement helps reduce stress on working mothers and strengthen family bonds without adding extra stress to students’ timetables.
Schools across the country are now redesigning their programmes based on these findings. **[I]** Instead of assigning theoretical worksheets, teachers invite parents and students to co-sign a simple weekly action plan. **[II]** This joint commitment ensures that classroom lessons are reinforced at home every evening. **[III]** At monthly review sessions, classes celebrate collective progress and exchange practical solutions to common obstacles. **[IV]**
The long-term implications of this partnership model are encouraging. When family members work side by side, <u>**they**</u> build mutual respect and lasting life skills. Ultimately, integrating sharing household chores and strengthening family bonds into both school curricula and family life prepares young citizens to thrive in an increasingly complex world.
(Adapted from National Educational Research Reports – Unit 1: Family Life)

**WHY CONSISTENCY MATTERS MORE THAN PERFECTION IN UNIT 1: FAMILY LIFE**
When people first decide to focus on sharing household chores and strengthening family bonds, they often set overly ambitious targets. Enthusiastic beginners might promise to transform their entire lifestyle in a single weekend, only to feel exhausted a few days later. Studies on habit formation show that well-paced household chores are far more effective when built step by step, helping family members teach children responsibility and teamwork without burnout.
The main reason crash campaigns fail is that <u>**they**</u> demand too much willpower at once. <u>**Small, consistent efforts practised every day produce far more lasting results than occasional bursts of intense activity.**</u> When a routine fits naturally into a family’s or student’s daily schedule, it requires less mental strain to maintain.
Experts therefore recommend a <u>**gradual**</u> approach to divide housework fairly at home. By starting with one simple task each day and celebrating weekly milestones, learners steadily build momentum. Such steady practice not only strengthens personal discipline but also helps communities reduce stress on working mothers and strengthen family bonds.
Of course, occasional setbacks are normal during busy exam weeks or family events. Rather than abandoning the goal altogether, resilient learners simply resume their routine the next morning, knowing that patience will <u>**foster**</u> long-term success.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 1: Family Life)

**Read the passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 17 to 26.**

**COMMUNITY ACTION AND PEER MENTORING IN UNIT 1: FAMILY LIFE**
Last year, youth unions in three provinces launched a six-month pilot programme to promote sharing household chores and strengthening family bonds at the grassroots level. Instead of relying on formal lectures, organisers trained two hundred high school volunteers to lead weekend activities where neighbours could divide housework fairly at home. Within the first two months, local communities reported <u>**tangible**</u> improvements in daily habits and neighbourhood solidarity.
A key factor behind this success was peer-to-peer mentoring. Teenagers often feel intimidated when adults lecture them, but they respond enthusiastically when classmates demonstrate how household chores can teach children responsibility and teamwork. By working in small teams of five or six, participants shared practical tips, solved everyday problems together and helped one another reduce stress on working mothers and strengthen family bonds.
Organisers also introduced simple tools to keep momentum high. **[I]** Every participating household received a visual progress board to track weekly milestones. **[II]** Local cultural centres hosted monthly gatherings where teams showcased their most creative ideas. **[III]** These celebrations turned routine tasks into a source of shared pride across the entire district. **[IV]**
Follow-up surveys conducted six months later confirmed that over seventy-five per cent of participants continued practising household chores independently. When student volunteers take ownership of community initiatives, <u>**their**</u> enthusiasm inspires both younger children and older residents. The pilot programme demonstrates that youth-led action is one of the most powerful ways to bring the values of Unit 1: Family Life to life.
(Adapted from Community Development & Youth Studies – Unit 1: Family Life)

qs.ex: tangible = rõ rệt, hữu hình, có thể nhận thấy thực tế (noticeable and real).

**COMMUNITY ACTION AND PEER MENTORING IN UNIT 1: FAMILY LIFE**
Last year, youth unions in three provinces launched a six-month pilot programme to promote sharing household chores and strengthening family bonds at the grassroots level. Instead of relying on formal lectures, organisers trained two hundred high school volunteers to lead weekend activities where neighbours could divide housework fairly at home. Within the first two months, local communities reported <u>**tangible**</u> improvements in daily habits and neighbourhood solidarity.
A key factor behind this success was peer-to-peer mentoring. Teenagers often feel intimidated when adults lecture them, but they respond enthusiastically when classmates demonstrate how household chores can teach children responsibility and teamwork. By working in small teams of five or six, participants shared practical tips, solved everyday problems together and helped one another reduce stress on working mothers and strengthen family bonds.
Organisers also introduced simple tools to keep momentum high. **[I]** Every participating household received a visual progress board to track weekly milestones. **[II]** Local cultural centres hosted monthly gatherings where teams showcased their most creative ideas. **[III]** These celebrations turned routine tasks into a source of shared pride across the entire district. **[IV]**
Follow-up surveys conducted six months later confirmed that over seventy-five per cent of participants continued practising household chores independently. When student volunteers take ownership of community initiatives, <u>**their**</u> enthusiasm inspires both younger children and older residents. The pilot programme demonstrates that youth-led action is one of the most powerful ways to bring the values of Unit 1: Family Life to life.
(Adapted from Community Development & Youth Studies – Unit 1: Family Life)

**Read the passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 33 to 40.**

**THE RIPPLE EFFECT OF PEER LEADERSHIP IN UNIT 1: FAMILY LIFE**
How do positive habits spread across a school or neighbourhood? Sociologists studying sharing household chores and strengthening family bonds have discovered that peer influence is often stronger than formal rules. When family members see their close friends willingly engage in household chores, they are far more likely to join in and teach children responsibility and teamwork.
Nevertheless, launching a new initiative is never without challenges. Organisers note that initial doubts and busy routines are common, and <u>**they**</u> can slow down participation during the first week. <u>**Young people learn most effectively when they observe respected peers applying positive habits in real-life situations.**</u>
For this reason, many schools encourage <u>**voluntary**</u> student ambassadors to lead by example. Whether demonstrating how to divide housework fairly at home or sharing practical tips during break time, these role models create a welcoming ripple effect that helps the whole school reduce stress on working mothers and strengthen family bonds.
Even when a minor <u>**obstacle**</u> arises, a supportive peer group keeps members motivated. What begins as the effort of a few enthusiastic students soon grows into a proud tradition shared by the entire community.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 1: Family Life)

peer influence and seeing close friends lead by example

**Read the passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 17 to 26.**

**OVERCOMING BARRIERS TO DAILY PRACTICE IN UNIT 1: FAMILY LIFE**
Why do many high school students agree that sharing household chores and strengthening family bonds is important, yet still find it difficult to divide housework fairly at home every day? Educational psychologists point out that modern teenagers face three main barriers: digital distractions, academic pressure and a lack of structured routines. When students feel overwhelmed, they often become <u>**reluctant**</u> to take on new responsibilities at home or in the community.
Fortunately, behavioural research shows that breaking large goals into micro-habits can overcome this hesitation. Instead of trying to change everything overnight, family members can start with a fifteen-minute daily routine focused on household chores. These manageable actions quickly build confidence and help learners teach children responsibility and teamwork without interfering with their homework.
Another effective strategy is using a structured weekly checklist. **[I]** When teenagers write down specific times and places for their tasks, they are three times more likely to follow through. **[II]** Sharing <u>**it**</u> with a supportive classmate or family member adds friendly accountability. **[III]** Rather than feeling pressured, students enjoy tracking their streak of completed tasks and seeing how their efforts reduce stress on working mothers and strengthen family bonds. **[IV]**
Teachers who have introduced micro-habits and checklists into their lessons on Unit 1: Family Life report remarkable improvements in student engagement. Once young people realise that small daily choices lead to meaningful results, household chores stops feeling like a burden and becomes a natural part of who they are.
(Adapted from Adolescent Psychology & Education Review – Unit 1: Family Life)
qs.q: The word **<u>reluctant</u>** in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to ______.
qs.ex: reluctant = ngần ngại, miễn cưỡng (hesitant and unwilling).

**Read the passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 17 to 26.**

**EXPERIENTIAL LEARNING AND THE FUTURE OF UNIT 1: FAMILY LIFE**
Across Viet Nam, forward-thinking high schools are transforming how students learn about sharing household chores and strengthening family bonds. Rather than treating Unit 1: Family Life as a set of vocabulary items to memorise for a test, teachers are integrating experiential learning into every week of the semester. Educators agree that hands-on practice is <u>**indispensable**</u> if young people are to teach children responsibility and teamwork.
In these classrooms, students work in project teams to investigate real issues and propose ways to divide housework fairly at home. For instance, learners might interview local residents, design bilingual awareness posters or organise a school-wide campaign on household chores. Through these authentic tasks, family members discover how their classroom English connects directly to everyday life.
Assessment methods are evolving alongside teaching styles. **[I]** Instead of relying solely on written quizzes, schools evaluate how effectively students collaborate and apply their plans. **[II]** Each team keeps a reflective portfolio documenting the challenges they faced and how their actions helped reduce stress on working mothers and strengthen family bonds. **[III]** This approach rewards creativity, persistence and genuine teamwork rather than rote memorisation. **[IV]**
Graduates of experiential programmes consistently report higher confidence when entering university and the workplace. Students <u>**who**</u> have practised solving real-world problems in high school adapt much faster to new environments. By making sharing household chores and strengthening family bonds an active, lived experience, education equips the next generation with both language proficiency and civic responsibility.
(Adapted from Modern Curriculum & Pedagogy Journal – Unit 1: Family Life)

qs.ex: indispensable = vô cùng cần thiết, không thể thiếu (essential and vital).

**EXPERIENTIAL LEARNING AND THE FUTURE OF UNIT 1: FAMILY LIFE**
Across Viet Nam, forward-thinking high schools are transforming how students learn about sharing household chores and strengthening family bonds. Rather than treating Unit 1: Family Life as a set of vocabulary items to memorise for a test, teachers are integrating experiential learning into every week of the semester. Educators agree that hands-on practice is <u>**indispensable**</u> if young people are to teach children responsibility and teamwork.
In these classrooms, students work in project teams to investigate real issues and propose ways to divide housework fairly at home. For instance, learners might interview local residents, design bilingual awareness posters or organise a school-wide campaign on household chores. Through these authentic tasks, family members discover how their classroom English connects directly to everyday life.
Assessment methods are evolving alongside teaching styles. **[I]** Instead of relying solely on written quizzes, schools evaluate how effectively students collaborate and apply their plans. **[II]** Each team keeps a reflective portfolio documenting the challenges they faced and how their actions helped reduce stress on working mothers and strengthen family bonds. **[III]** This approach rewards creativity, persistence and genuine teamwork rather than rote memorisation. **[IV]**
Graduates of experiential programmes consistently report higher confidence when entering university and the workplace. Students <u>**who**</u> have practised solving real-world problems in high school adapt much faster to new environments. By making sharing household chores and strengthening family bonds an active, lived experience, education equips the next generation with both language proficiency and civic responsibility.
(Adapted from Modern Curriculum & Pedagogy Journal – Unit 1: Family Life)

**SELF-REFLECTION AND LONG-TERM GROWTH IN UNIT 1: FAMILY LIFE**
Practising household chores is even more rewarding when learners take a few minutes each week to reflect on their progress. Educators studying sharing household chores and strengthening family bonds have found that students who keep a brief weekly journal understand their own habits much better and find it easier to teach children responsibility and teamwork.
During busy weeks, people sometimes miss a planned task or make mistakes. Without reflection, <u>**they**</u> may feel discouraged and assume that their efforts have failed. <u>**Honest self-reflection allows learners to turn early mistakes into valuable lessons rather than reasons to give up.**</u>
To make reflection effective, teachers recommend asking <u>**constructive**</u> questions every Sunday evening: What went well when we tried to divide housework fairly at home this week, and what small adjustment will help us improve next week?
Over time, this simple habit deepens personal <u>**commitment**</u> and helps family members reduce stress on working mothers and strengthen family bonds with confidence and pride.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 1: Family Life)
